title: The simplest thing that works
summary: Include people, failure recovery and future triggers in the cost of a design.

steps.title: Six services for a quiet product
steps.text: A team with four engineers proposes six services and a sharded database for a product serving 200 requests/s. Each service needs deployment, dashboards, contracts and someone to answer its pages. The diagram scales on paper, but the team is now the scarce resource. Simplicity means the fewest moving parts that meet the actual requirements, with a path to change.

steps.title: Put build and buy on the same horizon
steps.text: Compare three-year total cost, including engineering, infrastructure, support, upgrades, incidents, compliance work, egress and migration out. List which costs are assumptions. A managed service can charge more per unit and still save months of work. Building can win when control, unusual scale, residency or product differentiation justifies ownership. Check contracts, exit formats and operating limits before deciding. A modular service with a clear internal boundary may preserve future choices without a network boundary today. Do not shard just because the data may grow; measure write headroom, index size, maintenance time and recovery time first.

steps.title: Worked example: three years
steps.text: Assume loaded engineering cost of $180,000 per engineer-year. Building a specialized queue needs 0.5 engineer for year one and 0.2 for each of years two and three: 0.9 engineer-years, or $162,000. Add $2,000/month infrastructure for 36 months: $72,000. Total is about $234,000. Buying at $4,000/month costs $144,000. Add 0.1 engineer-year integration and 0.05/year operations for three years: $45,000, total $189,000. Buying is about $45,000 cheaper under these assumptions. A 50% vendor price rise applying to all 36 months would add $72,000 and reverse the result unless other costs change. This is a sensitivity exercise, not catalog pricing.

steps.q: A managed service costs twice the raw VMs. What is needed before comparing build and buy?
choices: VM costs plus initial implementation effort, excluding ongoing operations
A common ownership horizon including people, recovery and exit costs
Vendor fees versus VM cost after assuming equal maintenance effort
steps.why: Operating effort can differ substantially. Include it explicitly along with the guarantees each option meets.

steps.q: Your design seems too simple for year two. Follow-up: traffic grows tenfold.
checklist: Test 200 requests/s and the 2,000/s growth case with the actual write mix
Set a measured ceiling and allow time to migrate before reaching it
Include tested backups, restore targets and authorization initially
steps.model: I would show today's tested capacity, the tenfold case and where the first ceiling lies. At 200 requests/s, tenfold traffic is 2,000/s, which may still fit one well-indexed store depending on the write mix. I would avoid promising that without a benchmark. Stable keys, modular boundaries and exportable data leave room for a later split. I would fund the migration before measured headroom or recovery time crosses its trigger, while retaining backups and correctness from day one.

steps.title: A plan with triggers
steps.text: Month one: one deployable service, a transactional store, backups with a restore test, and basic user-outcome monitoring. Month six: add a cache or background queue only if measured latency or workload justifies it; keep the invariant in one place. Year two: split ownership or shard when an observed ceiling, team boundary or recovery target demands it. Start migration before forecast write utilization crosses the tested safe level or restore time exceeds the recovery objective. Include the time to migrate and verify, so the trigger leaves enough headroom. Keep identifiers, APIs and export paths ready for change. Simpler is not an excuse to omit durability, authorization or a viable rollback. The minimum design must still satisfy every binding requirement.

steps.q: One store meets tested peak and recovery targets. Which evidence most directly justifies planning a shard migration?
choices: The dataset doubled even though its tested working set and write load remain safe
Adding stateless API replicas requires adding the same number of database shards
Forecast headroom or restore time will cross a tested limit before migration can finish
steps.why: Use a measured ceiling and migration lead time. Data growth or API replica count alone does not establish a need to shard.

steps.q: Buying is cheaper in your table. Why might we still build? Follow-up: who owns it after launch?
checklist: Name a residency rule or missing guarantee that rules out the cheaper vendor
Assign a team capacity for upgrades, incidents and succession
Recalculate operating effort, migration-out cost and remaining risk
steps.model: A hard residency rule, a missing guarantee or a core differentiating feature could rule out that vendor. I would make the requirement explicit and revise the comparison, including the cost of meeting it ourselves. A named team needs capacity for upgrades, incidents and succession after the original authors leave. If we cannot staff that ownership, a more expensive supported option or a narrower product may be the responsible decision.

steps.q: A single service has backups but has never tested a restore. What is still unproven?
choices: Whether it can recover correct data within its recovery targets
Nothing, if every backup job reports success
Only recovery speed; a completed backup guarantees correct restoration
steps.why: Backup success does not establish restore correctness or duration. Test both against the recovery promise.

takeaway: Choose the smallest design that meets the promise, and attach measured triggers to future complexity.
